This person is a 24-year-old barista in London Zone 2 working zero-hours at a chain cafe, who wants any minimum wage rise to include a London weighting, guaranteed minimum weekly hours, a ban on unpaid 'trial' shifts, and stronger HMRC enforcement so on-call and pre-opening prep time is counted and paid.

This person is a small independent cafe owner in Camden employing 12 staff on tight margins, who argues for a two-year phased increase with quarterly steps, retention of lower youth and apprentice rates, permission to treat tronc/service charges as part of pay, and offsetting measures like a temporary cut to hospitality VAT and reduced employer NICs to avoid layoffs.

This person is a registered manager of a 70-bed care home in Teesside dependent on local authority fees, who supports raising the floor only if it is coupled to automatic, ring-fenced uplifts in council commissioning rates, explicit inclusion of travel time between home-care visits, and immediate adjustment of NHS and Skills for Care grants so they can match competitors without closing beds.

This person is a county council finance director in North Yorkshire responsible for adult social care budgets, who insists any increase be announced at least 12 months ahead and legally linked to corresponding increases in the Social Care Grant and Public Health Grant, plus flexibility on council tax caps or central top-ups to prevent cuts elsewhere.

This person is a 19-year-old apprentice electrician in Greater Manchester paying for tools and bus fare, who wants the lower apprentice rate scrapped after the first six months, mandatory payment of training and college hours at the full rate, and a travel allowance or tool grant funded alongside the wage rise so apprentices can afford to complete.

This person is a small-business owner of an eight-person electrical contracting SME in Salford who relies on apprentices, and advocates keeping a distinct apprentice rate with a slower glide path, paired with an apprentice wage credit or employer NIC rebate, and at least a six-month lead time so existing fixed-price contracts are not loss-making.

This person is a ride-hailing and delivery driver in Birmingham logged into apps 50 hours a week, who wants the policy to clarify that waiting and queuing time counts as working time, set a guaranteed per-hour floor across multi-app shifts, require algorithmic transparency on pay calculations, and fund HMRC to run proactive audits of platforms.

This person is a public policy head at a UK gig-economy platform, who argues for a sector code allowing per-job pay as long as average earnings meet the minimum over a defined shift window, a clear statutory definition of logged-in versus working time, a 12 to 18 month transition period, and credit against the floor for guaranteed earnings top-ups the platform already provides.

This person is a 72-year-old pensioner in rural Pembrokeshire on a fixed income who worries about wage-driven price pass-through on essentials, and favors smaller, predictable annual upratings tied to CPI with a sunset review, alongside temporary support like energy bill rebates if inflation spikes during implementation.

This person is a regional operations director for a major supermarket chain in the North West, who seeks a single national rate to reduce payroll complexity, a clear plan to manage pay compression for team leaders, at least six months' notice for price file and supplier renegotiations, and offsets such as temporary business rates relief to avoid pushing up shelf prices.

This person is a 27-year-old hotel housekeeper in London working split shifts on the current minimum wage; she wants any rise to include a London-weighted National Living Wage rate, mandatory pay for travel time and cleaning trolley setup between shifts, outlawing unpaid 'turnaround' minutes, stronger HMRC enforcement against wage theft, and coordination with Universal Credit so higher pay is not immediately lost to a steep taper.

This person is a small independent cafe owner in Hackney employing 12 staff; he supports a clear multi-year uplift timetable, but insists it be phased with at least 12 months' notice, keep differentiated apprentice and under-21 rates, raise the employer NICs threshold or give a small-firm rebate, clarify that service charges cannot be used to meet the wage floor, and provide temporary business rates relief to avoid cutting hours.

This person is a 45-year-old domiciliary care worker in Greater Manchester paid per visit with unpaid gaps; she wants the minimum wage rise to require councils and providers to count travel time between clients as working time, pay sleep-in shifts at least the new floor, reimburse mileage properly, and ring-fence central funding so contract rates rise enough that providers can pass through the wage increase.

This person is a local authority social care commissioning manager overseeing tight budgets in Salford; he wants any statutory increase to come with a dedicated central grant and a mandatory pass-through clause in contracts, a spring implementation date aligned to contract cycles, clear guidance on sleep-in obligations, and reporting requirements so providers evidence that uplifts reach frontline staff without destabilising the care market.

This person is a 22-year-old agency warehouse picker in the East Midlands on variable hours; he wants the new minimum to apply from day one for agency workers, require premium pay for night shifts above the floor, ban 'rolled-up' holiday pay practices, ensure paid rest breaks on long shifts, and mandate on-site audits for large fulfilment centres with a public naming-and-shaming regime for repeat offenders.

This person is a operations director for a regional logistics firm in Northamptonshire with 800 staff; she wants a predictable stepped schedule tied to Low Pay Commission recommendations, to retain lower youth and apprentice rates to protect entry-level hiring, clear rules so performance bonuses and piece rates sit on top of the wage floor without breaching it, and transitional support for energy and fuel costs that compound payroll pressures.

This person is a HM Treasury fiscal analyst and taxpayer who models distributional impacts; he wants the minimum wage uprating to be coordinated with Universal Credit taper adjustments and employee NIC and personal allowance thresholds to maximise take-home pay, to avoid region-specific rates that add compliance costs, to boost HMRC enforcement budgets, and to publish an inflation and employment impact assessment alongside the legislation.

This person is a director of a national anti-poverty charity based in Glasgow; she argues for a single Real Living Wage benchmark with a higher London supplement, abolishing lower youth and apprentice rates, strong joint-employer liability up supply chains so brands can't outsource low pay, automatic penalties and arrears with interest for underpayment, and living-wage conditions in all public procurement.

This person is a 58-year-old rural pub landlord in Cornwall running a seasonal business with live-in staff; he wants any increase to come in annually each April with two-year forward guidance, to raise the accommodation offset so tied lodging remains viable, to keep a distinct rate for 18-20 year-olds over the summer season, and to pair the change with a temporary VAT cut for hospitality to avoid reducing opening hours.

This person is a 19-year-old seasonal hotel housekeeper in Blackpool living in employer-owned accommodation; she wants the higher minimum to include a stricter cap on the accommodation offset so employers can't claw back wages, to remove lower youth rates for adults doing the same work, require that tips and service charges are paid on top of the wage floor, and to implement immediately rather than over multiple years.

This person is a 42-year-old domiciliary care worker in Leeds on a zero-hours contract who wants the minimum wage rise implemented with mandatory pay for travel time between clients, reimbursement for DBS checks and uniforms, and ring-fenced central government funding to councils so commissioned care rates cover higher wages; she cares because she routinely earns below the hourly minimum once unpaid travel is counted and fears agencies will cut visits unless local authority fees rise in step.

This person is a small home care agency owner in West Yorkshire employing 28 carers who supports a phased increase over 24 months only if the Department of Health and Social Care uplifts local authority contract rates by a specified per-hour amount, introduces a temporary employer National Insurance rebate for frontline care roles, and offers a hardship fund to prevent service disruption; he cares because 85% of his revenue comes from fixed council contracts that currently price below the proposed wage floor.

This person is a 19-year-old electrical apprentice in Birmingham who wants the apprentice rate abolished by year two of training, classroom days paid at the same hourly rate as on-site work, and a clear timetable aligning apprentice pay with the adult minimum by competency milestones rather than age; he cares because his rent and tools cost the same as older colleagues while his off-the-job hours are effectively paid less.

This person is a second-generation owner of a five-person electrical contracting firm in the West Midlands who argues the increase should preserve a lower first-year apprentice rate but pair it with government wage subsidies for off-the-job training hours, and tie progression to passing specific NVQ units; she cares because training two apprentices is essential to her pipeline but wage compression could make taking on trainees unaffordable without targeted support.

This person is a 24-year-old bartender in East London on a variable-hours contract who wants the minimum wage rise to include a London weighting, a ban on using service charges to meet wage floors, predictable scheduling rules with a premium for last-minute changes, and public naming of non-compliant employers; she cares because rent and transport costs outpace national averages and her rota is frequently cut with no compensation.

This person is a small independent restaurant owner in Hackney employing 16 staff who supports the rise if paired with a temporary VAT cut for hospitality or a time-limited employer National Insurance holiday up to the new wage floor, an increased accommodation offset for staff housing, and a six-quarter phase-in; he cares because payroll is already 45% of costs and a sudden jump risks closure before demand fully recovers.

This person is a human resources director at an NHS trust in Cornwall who wants any minimum wage uplift to come with a funded adjustment to the Agenda for Change pay spine to avoid pay compression at Bands 2–3, plus a dedicated Treasury allocation (including Barnett consequentials) so trusts are not forced to cut vacancies or services; she cares because unfunded rises automatically escalate bank and agency costs and destabilize recruitment.

This person is a policy analyst at a taxpayers' advocacy group in Surrey who argues the increase should be slower, indexed to clear Low Pay Commission productivity metrics, and paired with reforms to Universal Credit—raising work allowances and smoothing tapers—to target low-income households without loading costs onto public services; he cares about fiscal sustainability and preventing inflationary wage-price spirals from unfunded mandates.

This person is a community organizer in Lincolnshire working with seasonal migrant farm workers who wants the rise enforced through greater GLAA and HMRC budgets, mandatory digital timesheets in workers' languages, limits on the accommodation offset, and joint liability up the supply chain so supermarkets share penalties when labour providers underpay; she cares because she routinely sees piece-rate systems pushing effective pay below the legal minimum.

This person is a third-generation fruit grower in Kent who supports a modest, seasonal-phase implementation that protects lawful piece rates if average hourly pay meets the floor, raises the accommodation offset to reflect actual rural housing costs, and provides a harvest-time wage credit or DEFRA grant to offset the first year; he cares because margins are thin against imported produce and sudden cost spikes could wipe out the season.
